questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: Two failures that belong in different layers
questions.learningObjective: place a caller-fixable failure and a shared transient failure at different layers
questions.stem: A parse routine can fail in two ways: the text it was handed is malformed, which only the caller who supplied that text can correct, or the store it reads is briefly unreachable, which every caller would hit the same way. Where should each be handled?

options.text: Let the malformed-text failure travel up to the caller that supplied the text, and handle the unreachable store inside the routine, because only the caller can fix the text while every caller would otherwise repeat the same recovery
Handle both inside the routine, because a routine that can fail owes its caller a safe value on every path
options.misconception: believes a routine must convert every failure into an ordinary return value

options.text: Let both travel to the top, because one place that reports failures is easier to keep consistent than two
options.misconception: believes a single reporting layer beats fixing a failure where it can be understood

options.text: Handle the malformed text inside the routine, because the parse helper is the only place that knows the format
options.misconception: believes the shape of the text is a property of the helper rather than of the caller

questions.explanation: Where a failure is handled should follow who can act on it. The caller owns the text, so only the caller can decide whether to reprompt, reject the record, or accept a different format; reporting it as if the store were at fault sends the reader after the wrong thing. The unreachable store is nobody's input, and its recovery is the same for every caller, so it belongs inside the routine, once. Handling the text failure inside the routine is the tempting move, because the helper is where the format lives, but it leaves the caller unable to distinguish a bad record from a bad day.
questions.hint: Ask who can actually change the cause: the caller, or the routine.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: A message that names the cause against one that names the symptom
questions.learningObjective: judge two failure messages by whether the reader can act on the cause they name
questions.stem: Two messages report the same failed sign-in. The first says only that sign-in failed. The second says that no account matches this address and password pair. Which is the better report, and what does it buy the reader?

options.text: The second, because it names the condition that produced the failure, so the reader can tell a mistyped address from a wrong password and act on that difference instead of retrying blindly
The first, because a message that reveals nothing cannot be misused by anyone who sees it
options.misconception: believes that withholding detail is what makes a message safe

options.text: The second, because a longer message always gives the reader more to work with
options.misconception: believes message quality is a matter of length rather than content

options.text: The first, because naming the account lookup invites one address to be probed after another
options.misconception: believes that naming a check lets someone guess the values it checks

questions.explanation: The first names the symptom, which every failure in that area shares, so it cannot separate a mistyped address from a wrong password and leaves the reader with nothing but a retry. The second names the condition the routine actually tested, so it points at the specific step that did not match. Both can be written without disclosing anything sensitive, because the fact that a lookup found no match is not a secret; what matters is that the report distinguishes causes rather than merely sounding more technical.
questions.hint: Ask whether the two messages would lead a reader to different next steps.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: A message that carries a path, a line number, and a record identifier
questions.learningObjective: identify the three kinds of internal detail a raw failure report exposes
questions.stem: A payment page shows a raw failure report: a null fault at line 88 of OrderService, a record identifier, and a full path to an invoice file. What is wrong with this beyond its wording?

options.text: It hands over three things worth having — a file path, a line of internal source, and a stable record identifier — none of which the person reporting the problem needs in order to be helped
Nothing, because a technical report is the most precise description of the fault available
options.misconception: believes more internal detail always makes a report more precise

options.text: Only the path is a problem, because the other two details identify the failing record
options.misconception: believes a record identifier is safe to show because it is not a secret

options.text: The problem is only the language named, which makes the report look unprofessional
options.misconception: believes the offence is naming the language rather than the cause

questions.explanation: Each detail is a lever: the path shows how the system is laid out and where its data lives, the line number turns a report into a map of internal structure, and the record identifier is a handle that can be looked up by anyone who later gains access to the store. None of them helps the person who needs help, because what they can describe is what they were trying to do, which is enough for support to search on. The fix is not to shorten the report but to replace the internal detail with a handle that support can use privately.
questions.hint: Ask what a reader could do with each detail that they could not do from a plain description of the attempt.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: A correlation handle that finds the record without revealing it
questions.learningObjective: state what a correlation handle must and must not carry
questions.stem: A service returns a short opaque token with every failed request and writes the full internal detail in its log under that same token. What does the token buy, and what must it not contain?

options.text: It lets support find the exact log entry without exposing anything, so it must be unguessable and carry no path, account, or host of its own, since a guessable or descriptive token re-opens the leak it replaced
It lets the service skip writing the log, because the token already records what happened
options.misconception: believes the token replaces the written record rather than pointing at it

options.text: It speeds up the search through the log, because support can jump to the matching line
options.misconception: believes the token's value is speed rather than certainty about which entry is meant

options.text: It lets the user see why their own request failed, because the token decodes to the detail
options.misconception: believes an opaque token is a way of encoding the detail for the user

questions.explanation: The handle works because it is a join key, not because of anything it contains: the reader quotes it, support looks it up, and nothing sensitive crosses the boundary. That is also why its own content matters, because a token built from a timestamp, a counter, or a name carries structure that can be guessed and walked through. An unguessable token with no descriptive parts can be published to whoever needs it and still reveal nothing about the entry it names.
questions.hint: Ask whether the token could be guessed or read, and whether guessing it would expose anything.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: A message that stops before the remedy
questions.learningObjective: add the missing element that turns a rejection into something the reader can act on
questions.stem: A form rejects a birth date of 1904 with the words date out of range. The person at the keyboard cannot tell whether to retype it, ask someone, or simply try again later. What is missing?

options.text: The remedy: it should name what is accepted and what to do, for example enter a date between 1900 and today, so the reader can act without reading the source
Only the length, because a long message is easier to read than a short one
options.misconception: believes the fix is more words rather than a next step

options.text: The field name, because the person has to know which of six fields was rejected
options.misconception: believes naming the field is the same as saying what to do about it

options.text: Nothing, because a form that rejects bad input is behaving correctly on its own
options.misconception: believes correct rejection makes the message unnecessary

questions.explanation: A rejection that stops at the verdict leaves the work undone, because the reader's only route left is to guess what would be accepted. Naming the accepted range converts the report into an instruction, and it costs one clause. The field name is worth having but it is not the missing piece, since the person already knows which field they were filling in; what they cannot know is the bound that rejected it.
questions.hint: Ask what the reader would have to try next if the message were all they had.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: A value that is wrong against a call that failed
questions.learningObjective: explain why a wrong value and a failed call are not interchangeable to a caller
questions.stem: A routine hands back 0 when it cannot reach the store, and its caller adds that 0 to a running total as though it were a real reading. Why does the difference between a wrong value and a failed call matter here?

options.text: Because a wrong value is indistinguishable from a real one once it has been returned, so the caller cannot separate an honest 0 from a failure and the failure has to arrive by a different route than the value
It matters only for speed, because a failed call costs more time than a value lookup
options.misconception: believes the distinction exists to make the program faster

options.text: It does not matter, because both end up as a 0 in the total and the total is what is reported
options.misconception: believes two different causes are interchangeable once both are numbers

options.text: It matters because a failed call should be retried at once while a wrong value is recalculated
options.misconception: believes both failures deserve the same immediate retry

questions.explanation: The moment a failure is dressed as a value it loses the one property that made it recoverable: the caller can no longer tell it apart from a genuine reading, and every downstream step inherits that blindness. This is why failures travel on a separate route from results, so that a caller is forced to decide what to do about them. The total looks reasonable either way, which is exactly why the substitution survives review and is caught, if at all, by a reader comparing totals against counts.
questions.hint: Ask what the caller can still do after it has received the number.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: A marker value that is also a legal value
questions.learningObjective: locate the damage done when a marker sits inside the legal range of the data
questions.stem: A lookup returns -1 when the code is not found, and the codes in this system legally run from -1 to 99. What breaks, and where does the break actually show up?

options.text: The caller cannot tell not found from the real code -1, so the fault surfaces in the caller's test rather than in the lookup, and the marker has to move outside the legal range or be reported apart from the value
Nothing breaks, because the caller tests for -1 before it uses the result
options.misconception: believes a test on the marker suffices when the marker is itself a legal value

options.text: The lookup breaks, because it can no longer produce -1 once -1 is a legal code
options.misconception: believes the marker becomes unrepresentable inside the routine

options.text: The store breaks, because it refuses to hold a code equal to the marker
options.misconception: believes the marker is a restriction on storage rather than on the reading

questions.explanation: A marker only works in the space of values that cannot otherwise occur, and -1 here is a perfectly good code, so the caller's test is satisfied by both outcomes and the two collapse into one. The damage lands in the caller, which is why the routine itself keeps passing its own tests. The repair is to move the marker outside the legal range, or better, to report presence separately from the value, so that no value has to double as a signal.
questions.hint: Ask which of the legal values the caller's test cannot distinguish from the marker.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: A default that stands in for data nobody has
questions.learningObjective: trace how a substituted default turns a gap into a measurement
questions.stem: A reporting routine fills every missing reading with 0 and then averages over the full count of readings. A colleague asks why the average has come out low. What is the mechanism?

options.text: The substituted 0 is being treated as a measurement: it pulls the mean down and the denominator still counts the gap, so the routine reports a number nobody took and hides the fact that data was missing
The mean is low because the 0 is added twice, once as the filler and once in the sum
options.misconception: believes the substituted value is double counted rather than counted as a reading

options.text: The mean is low because the count of readings differs from the count of values summed
options.misconception: believes the denominator disagrees with the values being added

options.text: The mean is low because whole-number division drops the fraction at the end
options.misconception: believes the arithmetic type is at fault rather than the substituted value

questions.explanation: Filling a gap turns a known unknown into a false measurement, and the routine then treats it exactly like a real one in both the sum and the count, so the result is arithmetically correct and factually wrong. The tell is the count: a number derived from data that was never taken should change shape when the gap is closed, and here it does not, because the routine has no way left to say a reading was missing.
questions.hint: Ask whether the routine could still tell anyone that a reading was missing.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: A change that is half applied and never undone
questions.learningObjective: state what the caller needs when an operation stops between two writes
questions.stem: A transfer routine moves money out of one account and then fails while recording it in the other. What has to be true of the caller, and what does the tidier-looking alternative cost?

options.text: The caller must be able to tell that the transfer did not happen and must be able to put the first move back, because otherwise the two accounts disagree and nobody can tell which one to repair from the records alone
Nothing, because the second record is the one that matters and the first can simply be repeated
options.misconception: believes repeating a half-applied transfer repairs it

options.text: The caller must be told but nothing must be undone, because the first move is the smaller one
options.misconception: believes the size of the first change decides whether it needs reversing

options.text: The caller must run both writes again, because a half-finished change always completes on a second pass
options.misconception: believes a second attempt always finishes what the first one started

questions.explanation: A failure between two writes is not an error, it is a state: one account has been debited and the other has not been credited, and that state persists until somebody acts. The caller therefore needs two things, a way to learn that the pair is inconsistent and a way to reverse the half that happened. The tidier alternative, skipping the reversal because the first write was small, produces a mismatch that no later check attributes to this transfer, and by then the details needed to repair it are gone.
questions.hint: Ask what the records look like afterwards, and who could tell the two accounts apart.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: Checking a rule at the edge and again inside
questions.learningObjective: weigh the benefit of an inner check against the cost of a duplicated rule
questions.stem: The same rule, that a load must hold between 1 and 8 items, is checked in the request handler and again inside the loader that actually stores it. What does the second check cost, and when is it worth paying?

options.text: The inner check protects the loader from every caller, including the ones with no handler in front of them, and it costs a second copy of the rule that can drift from the first; it is worth paying when more than one path reaches the loader, provided the rule is written once and called twice
The inner check is pure waste, because the handler always runs before the loader is reached
options.misconception: believes one entry point makes every inner check redundant forever

options.text: The inner check is the only one that matters, because other callers bypass the handler
options.misconception: believes an outer check adds nothing even when the inner one already exists

options.text: The two checks are equivalent, because a rule checked twice must always give one verdict
options.misconception: believes repeating a rule stops the two copies from disagreeing

questions.explanation: Validation at the edge gives a good message to the person who made the request, and validation inside gives the routine a guarantee it can rely on without knowing its callers; these are different jobs and the second one is what makes the routine safe to use from anywhere. The cost is duplication, because two hand-written copies of a rule are two rules, and one of them will be changed without the other. A rule defined in one place and checked in both keeps the guarantee and removes the drift.
questions.hint: Ask who reaches the loader without passing through the handler.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: Failing fast or degrading, decided per call site
questions.learningObjective: justify different handling of one failure at two call sites
questions.stem: The same unavailable service is read by a dashboard that must render something and by a payment step that must be exactly right. Why should the two call sites treat that one failure differently?

options.text: Because the cost of a wrong answer differs at each site: the dashboard can show a marked-stale or cached reading, while the payment step must stop, since a guessed amount there is not something a later check can undo
They should not differ, because one consistent policy is easier to reason about than two
options.misconception: believes a uniform policy is always better than a suitable one

options.text: The dashboard should also stop, because a stale reading is a failure in disguise
options.misconception: believes degrading always hides something worse than stopping would

options.text: The payment step should degrade, because it can settle later while the person is present
options.misconception: believes a payment amount can be guessed now and corrected later

questions.explanation: The same cause produces different obligations, because what a caller owes the person in front of it varies: a display that admits staleness honestly is still useful, while a settled amount that was invented is not. Deciding this per call site, rather than once for the service, is what lets one be generous and the other strict. The temptation to standardise is strong because a single rule is easier to remember, and a single rule has to be the strictest one any caller needs.
questions.hint: Ask what each caller would have to tell the person if it guessed.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: An empty handler and what the caller then believes
questions.learningObjective: identify the false belief an empty handler leaves behind
questions.stem: A cache load is wrapped in a handler whose body is empty, so a failure returns whatever the routine already holds. What does the calling code now believe that is not true?

options.text: That it is holding fresh data: the empty handler makes failure look like an ordinary return, so a stale or empty value flows into the result and no later check can tell the difference
That the load succeeded, because raising nothing is what success looks like from outside
options.misconception: believes the absence of a raised error is evidence the data is current

options.text: That the cache is empty, because an empty body is the same thing as a cleared cache
options.misconception: believes an empty handler and an empty cache are one and the same state

options.text: Nothing false, because the value itself records whether it came from the cache
options.misconception: believes a returned value carries its own freshness

questions.explanation: An empty handler is a promise to the caller that nothing went wrong, made by code that knows something did. Everything downstream then reads the stale or empty value as current, because there is no signal left to contradict it, and the staleness is discovered by a person noticing an old figure rather than by the system. An empty handler is not the same as no handler: without one the failure travels and someone upstream must decide, and that decision is at least visible.
questions.hint: Ask what signal the caller has left that the data is not current.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: One report for four different rejections
questions.learningObjective: explain why a single collapsed test produces a single vague report
questions.stem: A routine reports invalid input for every value it rejects: a missing field, a field of the wrong type, a field out of range, and a duplicate. Why does one message serve all four cases?

options.text: Because the check was written as one test with one failure branch, so four distinct conditions collapse into one report; the fix is to test the conditions separately and say which one failed and what the caller should change
Because the caller cannot be told which field failed without seeing the whole record
options.misconception: believes the entire record has to be exposed to identify one bad field

options.text: Because all four cases are repaired the same way, so naming one adds nothing
options.misconception: believes different failures need no distinction when the repair might match

options.text: Because the routine never learns which field failed, as it is handed a whole record
options.misconception: blames missing knowledge instead of the single collapsed test

questions.explanation: The vagueness is a faithful report of the code, not of the data: one test with one exit cannot distinguish four reasons, so it reports one. Whoever has to fix the record then has to reproduce the whole check themselves to find out which condition applied, which is the work the check was supposed to save. Splitting the conditions costs a few lines and turns one useless report into four instructions, each naming its own remedy.
questions.hint: Ask how many failure branches the check has, and how many conditions it rejects.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: A broken guarantee relabelled as bad user input
questions.learningObjective: locate the layer that turned an internal fault into a user error
questions.stem: A reporting routine raises amount must be positive, and the interface above it turns every raised failure into you entered invalid data. What has gone wrong, and at which layer?

options.text: At the interface: it caught a condition about the program's own state and relabelled it as a fault in the person's input, so they are told to recheck something they never controlled and the real defect stays hidden
At the routine, because it should have returned a sentence rather than raising a failure at all
options.misconception: believes raising is wrong wherever a message could be returned instead

options.text: With the person, because a negative amount should never have been submitted in the first place
options.misconception: believes the caller typed the negative value and could retype it correctly

options.text: Nowhere, because translating a raised failure into a user message is what interfaces are for
options.misconception: believes any translation of a failure preserves what actually went wrong

The interface is where the damage happens, because that is where the meaning was changed, and the cost is that a real defect now looks like ordinary carelessness, so nobody investigates it. The routine that raised was behaving correctly; a report about internal state has to keep saying so as it travels up.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: A hold that only comes back on the happy path
questions.learningObjective: explain why a release has to sit on both the success and the failure path
questions.stem: A routine takes a hold on a file, reads it, and then does further work that can fail. Why must the release sit in a place that runs whether or not that work succeeded?

options.text: Because the hold is taken before the risky work begins, so any failure in between leaves it outstanding, and a release written only at the end is skipped by exactly the path that needed it most
It need not, because a failure ends the program and the hold is released as it exits
options.misconception: believes a failure always ends the whole program

options.text: It need not, because the hold is released when the routine's local name goes out of use
options.misconception: believes a local name going out of use releases what it holds

options.text: Only on the success path, because a failed read never took a hold worth releasing
options.misconception: believes a partial read leaves nothing that needs giving back

questions.explanation: The release has to be owned by the thing that took the hold, not by the last line of the success path, because the interesting failures are the ones that jump over the last line. A routine that returns early on a bad value, or that lets a failure travel out of the middle of its work, leaves the hold outstanding every time, and the number of outstanding holds only ever grows. The pattern that removes the reasoning entirely is to attach the release to the scope that took it, so no path can forget it.
questions.hint: Ask which line a failure jumps over on its way out.

questions.topic: Giving a hold back before the work it protects
questions.learningObjective: reason about the wrong order of two releases and the disagreement it creates
questions.stem: A routine writes a record into a cache and then notes the write in a log. The hold on the cache is given back before the note is attempted. What is inconsistent when the note fails?

options.text: The record is already outside the cache while the log still says nothing was stored, so the two disagree, and retrying the note alone cannot undo a write that has already left; the log's own hold has to be given back first
Nothing, because the cache copy is the record of truth and the log is only a note
options.misconception: believes one store's version settles the disagreement with the other

options.text: Only the order of the two log lines is wrong, because the record was still cached correctly
options.misconception: believes the position of a log line is the only thing the order affects

options.text: The cache hold cannot be given back at all, because it lasts until the log is written
options.misconception: believes a hold covers work carried out after it is released

questions.explanation: Order here decides which facts can still be true at the moment something goes wrong, and releasing first guarantees that a failure can leave the two stores telling different stories with no way back. The log records what the cache was believed to hold, so the log's own hold has to cover the cache work, not the other way round. This is the general shape: a handle stays held until everything it protects is safely recorded elsewhere.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: A cause that clears by itself against one that never will
questions.learningObjective: decide retryability from a property of the cause rather than from the wording
questions.stem: Two failures reach a caller. One says the far end refused the connection because it is overloaded; the other says the record that was asked for does not exist. Which is worth retrying, and what decides it?

options.text: Only the first, and the deciding property is whether the cause can change with nothing on the caller's side: an overloaded service clears by itself, while a record that is missing is missing just as much on the tenth attempt as on the first
Both, because retrying is always cheaper than reporting a failure to the person waiting
options.misconception: believes a retry costs nothing regardless of what caused the failure

options.text: Neither, because nothing in the failure itself says whether the cause is temporary
options.misconception: believes the wording of a failure carries no information about retryability

options.text: The first only if the caller can change something first, such as the size of the request
options.misconception: believes a temporary cause always depends on the caller's own request

questions.explanation: Retrying is worth doing when repeating the attempt could produce a different outcome, and the property that tells you is whether the cause is under anyone's control at the moment of the call. Overload is a state of the far end that clears; a missing record is a fact about the data that a repeat cannot alter, so the retry spends time and buys nothing. Encoding that property on the failure, rather than inferring it from the sentence, is what lets a retry policy be written once and trusted.
questions.hint: Ask what would be different on a second identical attempt.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: A code a program can match against a sentence it cannot
questions.learningObjective: explain what a stable code gives a caller that prose does not
questions.stem: A service reports failures as a short code such as quota exceeded, plus a sentence for people and the code for programs. What does the code give the caller that the sentence does not?

options.text: A stable handle to branch on: the code can be matched exactly, counted, and mapped to a remedy, while a sentence can be reworded or translated and matching on its wording then breaks without warning
A shorter message, so the code saves space on the wire for every failure
options.misconception: believes the value of a code is mostly how little it takes to send

options.text: A guarantee the failure cannot recur, because a code is only ever issued once
options.misconception: believes a one-off code means the cause is spent

options.text: A human-readable explanation, because the code stands in for the missing sentence
options.misconception: believes a code replaces prose for the person who reads it

questions.explanation: Prose is written for people and is therefore free to change: a rewording, a translation, or a shorter version for a small screen all break a program that was matching on it. A code is a contract, and its whole purpose is to be matched, counted, and mapped to a decision, which is why it changes only on purpose. The sentence still has to exist, because the person receiving it is the one who has to act, and the two are written for different readers of the same event.
questions.hint: Ask which of the two a translator or an editor is allowed to rewrite.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: Catching a kind of failure rather than a sentence
questions.learningObjective: say what catching by kind guarantees that catching by wording does not
questions.stem: A routine raises three separate kinds of failure and each is caught on its own, so the routine below can answer not found without ever touching the disk. What does catching by kind buy over catching by wording?

options.text: A guarantee that survives rewording: the kind is part of the identity of the failure, so each handler fires for every instance of its own condition and none of the others, with nobody matching on English text at all
A faster match, because comparing two kinds is quicker than comparing two sentences
options.misconception: believes the benefit is speed rather than reliability of the match

options.text: A shorter program, because one handler written generally can serve all three kinds
options.misconception: believes a single general handler is the shortened form rather than the blurred one

options.text: Nothing, because the wording is part of the failure and cannot change by accident
options.misconception: believes a message can never be reworded after the code is written

questions.explanation: Kinds are decided where the failure is raised, by the code that knows what went wrong, so a handler that names a kind is bound to the right condition however the reporting is later reworded. questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: Pairing a handler with the belief it leaves behind
questions.learningObjective: match each handler shape to what the caller is left believing
questions.stem: A cache read is wrapped so that a failure does not escape, and a colleague reads the report as though the figures were current. Which option pairs the handler with what the caller now believes?

options.text: Returning the last known value on failure: the caller believes the figures are current, and nothing downstream can show otherwise, because a returned value carries no news about its age
Raising with the age attached: the caller believes the figures are current, since the number is the same one as before
options.misconception: believes attaching an age stops a value from looking current

options.text: Raising with no detail: the caller believes nothing failed, because silence from a handler is a report of success
options.misconception: believes a handler that says nothing reports that all was well

options.text: Returning a default: the caller believes the figures are current, because the routine produced the value itself
options.misconception: believes a locally produced value is therefore a fresh one

questions.explanation: The age attached to the raised failure is the whole difference between the first pairing and the second, because it is the only one that leaves the caller able to say the figures are stale. Returning either the last known value or a default removes that information entirely, and a value that came from the routine's own code is no more evidential than one that came from the store. The rule that holds across all four is simple: if the caller may not act on the failure, the failure has to say so on the way out.
questions.hint: Ask what the caller can still learn about the value after the handler returns.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: Pairing a check with the guarantee it actually provides
questions.learningObjective: match each validation placement to the guarantee it gives and its cost
questions.stem: A rule says a load must hold between 1 and 8 items. Which option pairs a placement of the check with the guarantee it really gives?

options.text: Inside the loader as well as at the boundary: the loader is safe to call from anywhere, at the price of a second copy of the rule that has to be kept in step with the first
At the boundary only: the loader is safe to call from anywhere, because every request passes the boundary
options.misconception: believes one entry point covers every possible caller

options.text: In both places: there is no cost at all, because a check that runs twice costs nothing
options.misconception: believes duplicated rules carry no cost in keeping them alike

options.text: Nowhere, trusting the caller: the rule still holds, because a trusted caller cannot send a bad load
options.misconception: believes trust makes a check unnecessary

questions.explanation: A guarantee belongs with the routine that depends on it, which is why the inner check is the one that makes the loader safe for any caller, and why the boundary check is a courtesy to the person rather than a guarantee about the store. The price is a second copy, and copies drift, so the workable version defines the rule once and has both layers call it. Trusting the caller is the version that works exactly until a second caller appears.
questions.hint: Ask which of the two checks is protecting a routine rather than a person.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: Why resetting state to survive a failure hides the failure
questions.learningObjective: argue that discarding running work removes the evidence of the fault
questions.stem: A loop catches a failure and sets its running total back to zero so that the run can continue. Explain, in a short paragraph, why this hides more than the one failure.

answer.exemplar: The reset does not remove the failure, it removes the evidence of it. The total was the only record of the work done before the failure, so clearing it also clears the fact that the work happened, and the run continues from a number that looks like a deliberate starting point rather than the wreckage of a fault. Anyone reading the result afterwards sees a total that is simply wrong, with no mark at the point where it stopped making sense and nothing to connect it to the row that caused the trouble. A handler that keeps the work so far and records the failure at that point preserves both the answer and the diagnosis, whereas the reset keeps neither.

questions.explanation: A strong answer names the total as the only record of the work before the failure, says that clearing it destroys the link between the wrong result and the point where it went wrong, and concludes that the reset converts a locatable failure into an unattributable wrong number. An answer that only says the total becomes inaccurate stops one step short, because inaccuracy is a fault everyone can see and does not explain why the fault cannot be traced. The best answers also contrast the two designs, keeping the partial work and recording the failure, against discarding it and carrying on as though the count had simply started there.
questions.hint: Ask what the running total is evidence of, and what clearing it removes.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: What a readable handle gives away
questions.learningObjective: argue that a handle gains nothing from being human readable
questions.stem: A support handle is built from a timestamp and a counter so that it reads neatly in a log. Explain, in a short paragraph, what that choice gives away and why the readability is not worth it.

answer.exemplar: A handle made of a timestamp and a counter can be reconstructed by anyone who can see one example of it, because both parts are small in range and both follow a known order. That turns the handle from a lookup key into a window: guess the second part near a time the person already mentioned, and a stream of entries can be read without any access at all. Readability is also not really gained, since a person reading a log gains nothing from a handle that resembles the other handles around it. An unguessable handle with no descriptive parts can be quoted to support in public and still reveal nothing about the entry it names, which is the only property the handle has to have.

questions.explanation: A good answer names the two parts as a small search space that anyone can enumerate, connects that to reading entries they were never given, and then makes the point that readability buys nothing, because a person gains no information from a handle that looks like its neighbours. An answer that stops at the handle is guessable has not finished, since guessable is the first step and the consequence is what matters: whole log entries, not just numbers. The strongest answers finish with the requirement itself, unguessable and undescribed, since that is the whole job of a handle.
questions.hint: Ask what a reader could build from a handle they were given, and what they would then be able to read.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: Why a wrong layer costs more than a vague message
questions.learningObjective: argue that mislabelling a failure at an interface destroys the diagnosis
questions.stem: One interface turns every raised failure into the same sentence telling the person they entered invalid data. Explain, in a short paragraph, why this costs more than a vague message inside a single routine.

answer.exemplar: A vague message inside a routine is wrong in one place, and the person who reads it can still see from its shape that something is being described badly. An interface that relabels every failure changes what the failure means at the moment it travels, so the information is destroyed at the one point where several different causes are still distinguishable. Everything above the interface then sees a fault in the person's input, which means the real cause is never looked for and the defect that produced it is free to happen again. The cost is not a worse sentence, it is the loss of the distinction between a fault in the request and a fault in the program, which is the distinction that tells anyone where to look.

questions.explanation: A strong answer identifies the interface as the point where several causes are still distinguishable and the collapse happens, and it says what the collapse destroys, which is the ability to tell a fault in the request from a fault in the program. An answer that only says the message is unhelpful stops short, because the same words inside one routine are merely vague. The best answers also carry the consequence through, that nobody investigates a defect that looks like carelessness, and add what the interface should do instead, keep the cause and pass it on in the terms of the thing that actually failed.
questions.hint: Ask how many different causes the interface is merging, and what the reader is left able to conclude.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: What the boundary check and the inner check are each for
questions.learningObjective: separate the two jobs that two checks of one rule are doing
questions.stem: A rule about how many items a load may hold is checked in the request handler and again inside the routine that stores it. Explain, in a short paragraph, what each of those two checks is for.

answer.exemplar: The check in the handler exists for the person who made the request: it can reject the value while the person is still there, and it can say what would be accepted, which is a message only a boundary can give. The check inside the storing routine exists for whoever calls it: it makes the routine safe to use from a path with no handler in front of it, such as a scheduled job or another routine, and it costs almost nothing because a rejected value cannot reach the storage. They are not duplicates of one job, and the cost of having both is not the running of two checks but the maintenance of two copies of a rule that can be changed in one place and left alone in the other.

questions.explanation: A good answer gives each check a different beneficiary, the person at the boundary and the routine that depends on the rule, and says why the inner one cannot be dropped when a second caller exists. An answer that calls them redundant has missed the point, since redundancy is judged against the callers rather than against the checks. The strongest answers name the real cost as two copies of one rule drifting apart, and finish with the arrangement that keeps both guarantees, one rule written once and called from both places.
questions.hint: Ask who each check is protecting, and what each one can say that the other cannot.
